title: The Orphan of the Isère and the Cities on Paper: Bouvard from the Champ-de-Mars to the Río de la Plata
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Saint-Jean-de-Bournay, the plasterer's son
stops.date_confidence: attested. fr.wikipedia gives the day, month and year, and the reading is consistent with D'Elboux's thesis and with the italyworldsfairs.org profile. Coordinates corrected from the pool's figure to the commune's own, about a kilometre south of it.
stops.campa: In a small town of the Isère, on the nineteenth of February, a plasterer aged twenty-two and his wife Madeleine Rostaing have a son and give him the father's name. The house is a working house and the trade is lime, sand and the flat of a trowel. Nothing in the parish suggests that this child will fix where the Grand Palais stands, or draw boulevards for a sultan, or sign the plan that turns Buenos Aires toward its river. He is Joseph Bouvard, son of Joseph Bouvard, and the father has three years left to live.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard'
Roseli Maria Martins D'Elboux, doctoral thesis, FAU-USP, abstract at teses.usp.br
suggested_refs: The civil birth register of Saint-Jean-de-Bournay, Isère, 19 February 1840, in the departmental archives

stops.name: Vienne, orphaned twice before fourteen
stops.date_confidence: mixed. The father's death about 1843 and the mother's remarriage to the wheelwright Gaspard Laurent at Vienne in 1844 are attested by fr.wikipedia. The mother's death in 1853 is reconstruction, compilation tradition rebuilding the Legion d'honneur service file, with no primary act located; the stop is dated to the orphaning year only to order the segment.
stops.campa: The father dies when the boy is three. His mother remarries a wheelwright of Vienne, Gaspard Laurent, and the household moves to the old Roman town on the Rhône, where a half-brother, Florentin, is born into it. Then the mother dies too, and at thirteen he belongs to nobody. He attends the collège of Vienne. Around him stand the arch, the pyramid of the circus, the temple of Augustus and Livia with its columns twenty centuries old, and a boy with no inheritance learns to draw them.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard'
Compilation tradition reconstructing his Legion d'honneur service statement, per D'Elboux
suggested_refs: The civil registers of Vienne, Isère, for the deaths of Joseph Bouvard the elder and Madeleine Rostaing

stops.name: Vienne, the office of Hugues Quenin
stops.date_confidence: the apprenticeship is attested by fr.wikipedia, which calls him a pupil of Hugues Quenin, architect at Vienne, and gives no year at all; 1855 is a reconstruction and dates the stop only to order the segment. That Constant-Dufeux noticed him during restoration work at the Roman temple is tradition, supported by no contemporary letter or diary in any source reached.
stops.campa: He enters the office of Hugues Quenin, architect of the City of Vienne, and learns the trade the way the trade was learned: measuring, tracing, copying antique orders in ink. Tradition puts the turn of his life at the Temple of Augustus and Livia, where a visiting Parisian, Simon-Claude Constant-Dufeux, is at work on the Roman fabric and looks over the shoulder of a draftsman with no money and no family. The picturesque part of the story has no letter behind it. What is certain is that the draftsman leaves for Paris.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard'
italyworldsfairs.org biographical profile, which confirms the Quenin training but mislocates it in Vienna, Austria
suggested_refs: The Temple of Augustus and Livia at Vienne, and the nineteenth-century restoration files of the City of Vienne

segments.name: The City of Paris Takes Him In

stops.name: Hôtel de Ville, attached to the architecture service
stops.date_confidence: the attachment to the City of Paris architecture service in 1864 is attested by fr.wikipedia; the exact day of 30 August comes from the compilation tradition around the unviewed Legion d'honneur file and is a reconstruction. The pin is the canonical Paris pin at the Hôtel de Ville.
stops.campa: At twenty-four he is taken onto the architectural staff of the City of Paris, the enormous municipal machine the prefecture has built to cut, pave, drain and rebuild a capital. He will not leave it for forty-seven years. Sub-inspector, inspector, architect of the permanent service, inspector general, administrative director: he climbs every rung of it, and the climb takes the whole of his working life. He is a salaried employee of a municipality before he is a student of architecture.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard'
fr.wikipedia, 'Avenue Joseph-Bouvard', which describes his final post
suggested_refs: The personnel registers of the City of Paris architecture service, Archives de Paris

stops.name: École des Beaux-Arts, admitted to Constant-Dufeux's atelier
stops.date_confidence: the year 1864 and the atelier of Constant-Dufeux are attested by fr.wikipedia, and the two 1865 medals with them. The exact day of 1 December, the second-class admission and matriculation number 2260 are reconstructions resting on Archives nationales dossier AJ/52/357, which was not viewed in this research.
stops.campa: Rue Bonaparte admits him to the second class, into the atelier of the master who had found him at Vienne. He is already a municipal employee, so the school is the second half of a double education, one half at the office and one at the board. The next year he takes two medals, one for a project in timber construction and one for perspective: how a thing stands up, and how it looks to somebody walking toward it. The register gives his matriculation number as 2260.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard'
Archives nationales, dossier AJ/52/357, cited in the compilation tradition but not consulted here
suggested_refs: The matriculation registers of the École impériale et spéciale des Beaux-Arts, Archives nationales AJ/52

stops.name: Buzenval, wounded in the siege
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The wound is attributed to his Legion d'honneur service file as summarized by D'Elboux, and fr.wikipedia's Bouvard article does not mention it at all. The pool dated it to November 1870, when no action took place at Buzenval; fr.wikipedia's Bataille de Buzenval gives exactly two engagements, 21 October 1870 and 19 January 1871. The later date is used to order the segment and no source chooses between them. Coordinates corrected; the pool's figure fell near Mont-Valérien.
stops.campa: Paris is ringed and starving, and the architects are in uniform with everybody else. In the park of Buzenval, west of the city, the garrison tries twice to break the German lines and fails twice, leaving the slopes covered with national guardsmen who had never fought before. Bouvard is wounded there. The only document that says so is a service statement drawn up years later for a decoration file. It gives no unit and no date, and it does not say what the wound was.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Bataille de Buzenval', which fixes the only two engagements
Compilation tradition citing his Legion d'honneur service record, not independently viewed
suggested_refs: Base Léonore, Legion d'honneur dossier of Joseph-Antoine Bouvard, Archives nationales

stops.name: Palais du Luxembourg, under Davioud after the siege
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: compilation tradition drawing on the INHA authority record and the Legion d'honneur file, neither of which could be opened, AGORHA returning 403 on every attempt. Coordinates corrected to the palace itself; the pool's figure sat inside the garden.
stops.campa: Two weeks after the armistice, and with the Commune still ahead, he is put under Gabriel Davioud, the man who gave Paris its fountains, its theatres on the Châtelet and the furniture of its parks, to work on the adaptation of the Luxembourg Palace. It is the apprenticeship that counts for more than the school. Davioud belongs to Alphand's circle and Alphand to Haussmann's, and Bouvard is now inside the line of descent. The assignment is dated the first of February.
sources: Compilation tradition, INHA-derived; agorha.inha.fr returned 403 and could not be checked
fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard' for the municipal career
suggested_refs: The post-siege works accounts of the Palais du Luxembourg under Gabriel Davioud

stops.name: Marly-le-Roi, the household
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout. The marriage of 12 November 1874 to Clarisse Agathe Hélène Basselier and the birth of the son on 1 October 1875 rest on the INHA authority record, which returned 403 on every attempt; no civil act was inspected. Coordinates standardised on Nominatim's figure for Marly-le-Roi, the pool having carried two different ones for the same village.
stops.campa: He marries Clarisse Agathe Hélène Basselier and takes a house at Marly-le-Roi, in the woods west of Paris where the demolished palace of the Sun King has left only water and terraces. A son is born there in October, Charles Louis Roger, who will be an architect in his turn and will one day walk through Constantinople at his father's side. Everything about this household reaches us through a card in an authority file: a marriage date, a birth date, a village. Bouvard keeps the house for forty-five years and dies in it.
sources: Compilation tradition drawing on the INHA authority record, inaccessible (403)
fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph Bouvard', for the son Roger Bouvard
suggested_refs: The civil registers of Marly-le-Roi, Seine-et-Oise, for the marriage of 1874 and the birth of 1875

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the pavilion of the City of Paris
stops.date_confidence: attested. fr.wikipedia gives the Chevalier of the Legion d'honneur in 1878, and the pavilion attribution is independently carried by the italyworldsfairs.org profile, fetched before that host became unreachable. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: France stages a world's fair to prove it has recovered from the war and the Commune, and the City of Paris wants a building of its own inside it. Bouvard designs it: iron, colour, glazed ceramic, the municipality showing itself off as a modern body with drains and schools and gasworks. It is his first building on the Champ-de-Mars and it is built to be taken down again, which is what happens when the fair closes. He is thirty-eight, and he is made Chevalier of the Legion of Honour for it.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard' for the 1878 decoration
italyworldsfairs.org profile, which states that Bouvard designed the Paris City Pavilion for 1878
suggested_refs: Photographs and plates of the Pavillon de la Ville de Paris, Exposition Universelle of 1878

segments.name: Barracks, Stations, Schools, and a Dome

stops.name: Hôtel de Ville, architect of the permanent service
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: fr.wikipedia carries the appointment and its date as career summary without a document, and the prefectural order was not seen. The seat on the ministry's committee for school buildings, dated 1880 in the pool, is on the same footing.
stops.campa: The city makes him permanent. It is the difference between a man employed on works and a man who is part of the administration, with a title, a district and a claim on the next opening above him. In the same season the state takes him too: government architect, and a seat on the ministry's committee for school buildings. Within a few years the ministry will hand him a technical school to build in the mountains of that same Isère, in a town thirty kilometres from the one he was born in.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard'
Compilation tradition for the ministerial committee, unconfirmed against any appointment record
suggested_refs: Prefectural orders of the Seine on the architecture service, Archives de Paris

stops.name: Caserne Louviers, barracks on the boulevard Morland
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the barracks appear in the compilation lists of his works, including the italyworldsfairs.org profile, but the City of Paris municipal records behind the attribution were not fetched. Dated to the start of works given in the pool, 1882-1883; month and day unknown.
stops.campa: On the filled ground of the old Île Louviers, swallowed by the quay a generation earlier, he builds barracks for the Republican Guard. It is the unglamorous half of municipal architecture and the half that pays: stables, dormitories, a yard, a façade that has to look like the Republic without costing what the Republic costs. Between the monuments and the expositions this is the work that fills his decade, and almost none of it carries his name where a passer-by can read it. The building goes up on the boulevard Morland between 1882 and 1883.
sources: Compilation tradition citing City of Paris municipal architectural records, not fetched
italyworldsfairs.org profile, listing the Caserne de la Garde Républicaine of 1882-1883
suggested_refs: City of Paris works dossiers for the Caserne Louviers, boulevard Morland

stops.name: Voiron, the national vocational school
stops.date_confidence: the architect attribution is attested by fr.wikipedia, which dates the work loosely to around 1885. The dates used here are the school's own: creation by decree of 26 July 1882 and opening on 5 October 1886, per fr.wikipedia's École nationale professionnelle. The pool's claim that Voiron was the first national vocational school in France is false, Vierzon having been decreed on 9 July 1881; Voiron was the first to open, since Vierzon opened only in 1887. Coordinates corrected to the school building.
stops.campa: The Republic wants schools that turn peasants' sons into fitters and draughtsmen, and it decrees four of them. Voiron takes the second decree and opens first, and the man who draws it is a boy from thirty kilometres away who was orphaned at thirteen and put into an architect's office because there was nothing else to do with him. He builds workshops, drawing halls, dormitories, a courtyard. The building is still a school. Its first pupils are the class he came out of.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard'
fr.wikipedia, 'École nationale professionnelle', for the decree of 26 July 1882 and the opening of 5 October 1886
suggested_refs: The Lycée polyvalent Ferdinand Buisson, Voiron, the former École nationale professionnelle

stops.name: Place Malesherbes, the setting for Dumas
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: City of Paris monument records, not fetched. The pool places on the same evidential footing two neighbouring commissions, decorative motifs for the Place de la République with Ulysse Gravigny in 1881 and the architectural setting of the Diderot monument on the boulevard Saint-Germain with the sculptor Jean Gautherin in 1886. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: Gustave Doré, better known for engraving hells and forests, models a seated Alexandre Dumas with his readers heaped below him and d'Artagnan standing guard behind. Bouvard supplies the ground it stands on: the pedestal, the steps, the way the square receives the figure. The bronze is signed. The setting is not, and a whole department of his practice looks like this: other men's monuments standing on his arrangements, on municipal ground he controls.
sources: Compilation tradition citing City of Paris monument records, not independently fetched
suggested_refs: The monument to Alexandre Dumas by Gustave Doré, Place du Général-Catroux, formerly Place Malesherbes

stops.name: Saint-Étienne, the station on hydraulic jacks
stops.date_confidence: attested by archives.saint-etienne.fr for the hydraulic-jack system, the iron armature and the opening of 27 October 1884, with construction running 1884-1886. Two cautions from that same page: it names the architect only as M. Bouvard, so the identification rests on the compilation tradition; and its figure of 1.80 metres of subsidence describes the settling of the earlier station over twenty years, which is why it was rebuilt, not an allowance designed into the new one.
stops.campa: Under Châteaucreux the coal has been cut away for a century and the ground goes down. The station standing there has sunk nearly two metres in twenty years, so they pull it down, and Bouvard rebuilds it on an iron armature seated on hydraulic jacks, so that when the earth drops again the building can be screwed back to level. The jacks are the whole design decision and they sit under the floor, where none of the passengers will ever see them. The station opens on the twenty-seventh of October 1884, with the works still running.
sources: archives.saint-etienne.fr, Gare de Châteaucreux, which confirms the jacks, the armature and the opening date
suggested_refs: The Gare de Saint-Étienne-Châteaucreux, Square Stalingrad, and the municipal archive dossier on its rebuilding

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the dome opposite the tower
stops.date_confidence: attested for the gold medal, the promotion to Officier of the Legion d'honneur in 1889 and the attribution of the Palais des Industries: fr.wikipedia's Exposition universelle de 1889 states that the Palais des Industries was fitted out by Joseph Bouvard, giving the Galerie des Machines to Contamin and Dutert, while fr.wikipedia's own Bouvard article makes the confusion the other way. The appointment date of 31 July 1886 is a reconstruction; the opening day of the fair places the stop. The quoted lecture is dated 1887 only, the pool's 7 April being unsupported.
stops.campa: Eiffel puts up three hundred metres of open iron at one end of the field. At the other, Bouvard raises the Palais des Industries diverses and crowns it with a central dome of metal, glass, gilding, painted allegory and coloured ceramic, and the ceremonies of the fair turn around it. Huysmans, who prefers his iron naked, calls the polychromy heavy and conventional. Bouvard takes the exposition's gold medal and the cross of an Officier. The tower is still there. The dome came down with the rest.
stops.quote: Eu acreditava ingenuamente que aqueles que executam ou que produzem pessoalmente eram os melhores mestres para se aprender a executar e a produzir; cheguei mesmo a pensar que esses seriam os únicos capazes de o fazer. [...] Quando fui honrosamente convidado a preparar um estudo sobre a próxima exposição, achei a coisa muito simples, natural mesmo, e, ainda imbuído de minhas velhas ideias, considerei que frente a um assunto tão vasto e, em razão de minha colaboração direta nessa obra, não seria difícil de vos entreter durante uma hora.
stops.quote_source: Bouvard's lecture on the coming Exposition of 1889, in Conférences sur la science et l'art industriel (Paris, 1887), pp.507-536, in the Portuguese translation of Roseli Maria Martins D'Elboux, Revista Brasileira de História da Ciência 11(1), 2018, p.38 n.4; the French original could not be located
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Exposition universelle de 1889'
fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard' for the 1889 decoration
D'Elboux 2018, for the 1887 lecture
suggested_refs: J.-K. Huysmans on the polychromy of the central dome, in his Salon and exposition criticism of 1889

stops.name: Paris, succeeding Alphand
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a tag deliberately downgraded. Alphand died on 6 December 1891, not in 1892, and fr.wikipedia's Bouvard article says only that Bouvard succeeded him, giving no year at all, so the pool's attested 1892 was unsupported. Read as 1891-1892 and placed at the canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: Adolphe Alphand dies in December, and with him the last of the men who cut the Bois de Boulogne into shape and hung the parks on Haussmann's boulevards. The city gives Bouvard the administrative direction of architecture, and in time the promenades and plantations with it: every tree, every bench, every square, every municipal building in Paris under one signature. Later writers will make him Haussmann's disciple. He never worked for Haussmann. He inherited the chair of the man who did.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Jean-Charles Alphand', for the death of 6 December 1891
fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard', which names the succession but no year
suggested_refs: The reorganisation of the City of Paris services of architecture, promenades and plantations after Alphand

stops.name: Bourse du Travail, rue du Château-d'Eau
stops.date_confidence: attested: fr.wikipedia's Bourse du travail de Paris gives Joseph-Antoine Bouvard as architect, construction from 1888 to 1896, inauguration in May 1892, the three allegorical heads and the wood-and-iron hall. The day within May is not given and is defaulted to the first. Coordinates corrected to that article's own figures.
stops.campa: The municipality builds the organized workers a house of their own, and Bouvard gives it a Renaissance front with the trades cut into the stone and three heads over the door: Labour, Peace, the Republic. Behind them a great hall of wood and iron where the unions meet. The century's argument is written into the elevation, a syndicalist assembly dressed in the architecture of an exchange. It is inaugurated in May 1892 with four more years of works still to run.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Bourse du travail de Paris'
suggested_refs: The Salle Ambroise-Croizat, the iron-framed meeting hall of the Bourse du Travail, 3 rue du Château-d'Eau

stops.name: Marseille-Saint-Charles, the U around the glass roof
stops.date_confidence: attested: fr.wikipedia's Gare de Marseille-Saint-Charles states that the present station was built from 1893 to 1896 by the architect Joseph-Antoine Bouvard, and describes the U-shaped plan around its glazed roof. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: High on the Saint-Charles plateau, with the city dropping away below it toward the water, he rebuilds the terminus of the line from Paris: a U of buildings closed around a great glazed hall, the trains ending under glass and the passengers walking out onto a platform above Marseille. It is his second station and the same problem as the first, a machine shed obliged to behave like a civic monument, solved here with no jacks underneath it. He is fifty-three and directing the architectural services of Paris while it goes up.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Gare de Marseille-Saint-Charles'
suggested_refs: The 1893-1896 station buildings and glazed hall of Marseille-Saint-Charles

stops.name: Grand Palais and Pont Alexandre III, directing the fair of 1900
stops.date_confidence: attested: fr.wikipedia gives the 1897 appointment as director of architecture and festivals and the promotions to Commandeur and then Grand Officier of the Legion d'honneur, and the Petit Palais object record independently describes him as director of the architectural works of the Exposition of 1900. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: For the fair of 1900 he is not the designer of the monuments but the man who decides where they go. He fixes the siting of the Grand Palais and the Petit Palais and the bridge thrown between them, and he coordinates a temporary city along both banks of the Seine: pavilions, lighting, water, the calendar of festivities. Of the whole temporary city only the two palaces and the bridge are built to last. Millions walk through an arrangement that is his. He is given a Grand Prix and raised to Grand Officier of the Legion of Honour.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard'
parismuseescollections.paris.fr, which calls him directeur des travaux d'architecture de l'Exposition universelle de 1900
suggested_refs: The general plan of the Exposition Universelle of 1900 along both banks of the Seine

stops.name: Petit Palais, the face Flameng drew
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Petit Palais object record: François Flameng, 1900, ink wash and gouache on paper, inscribed to Monsieur Bouvard, inv. PPD5844. One correction to the pool: the record says the decorative scheme at the Conservatoire des arts et métiers for which the drawing was made was destroyed in 1965, not the Conservatoire, which still stands and is still an institution. The stop sits at the drawing's present home; month and day unknown.
stops.campa: François Flameng draws him in ink wash and gouache and writes across the sheet, To Monsieur Bouvard. The inscription is in capitals and the sheet is signed. The drawing is made for a decorative scheme at the Conservatoire des arts et métiers; the scheme is destroyed in 1965 and the sheet outlives it, catalogued at the Petit Palais under a number, describing him in the museum's own words as director of the architectural works of the Exposition of 1900. No other likeness of him has surfaced.
sources: parismuseescollections.paris.fr, 'Portrait de Joseph Bouvard', inv. PPD5844
suggested_refs: François Flameng, Portrait de Joseph Bouvard, 1900, Petit Palais, musée des Beaux-Arts de la Ville de Paris

stops.name: Paris, the cross given to his half-brother
stops.date_confidence: attested: fr.wikipedia records that Florentin Laurent received the Legion d'honneur from the hands of his brother Joseph-Antoine Bouvard on 28 November 1900. The place of the ceremony is not given in the source, so the stop sits at the canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: Fifty-six years after a wheelwright of Vienne married his widowed mother, Bouvard pins the cross of the Legion of Honour on that wheelwright's son. Florentin Laurent takes it from the hands of his own brother, on the twenty-eighth of November, in the year the fair made Bouvard a Grand Officier of the same order. Both halves of the family, the orphan carried off to Paris and the one who stayed in the Isère, stand in the same room for an afternoon. The record of the day calls them brothers without qualification.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph-Antoine Bouvard', citing the award to Florentin Laurent on 28 November 1900
suggested_refs: Base Léonore, Legion d'honneur dossier of Florentin Laurent

stops.name: Paris, the river he wanted to open
stops.date_confidence: attested as a quotation: Bouvard's own words in Le Temps of 17 June 1904, p.458, reproduced in Alicia Novick's article of 2000, whose PDF was fetched and read. Novick reads this river-garden project as the precedent for the riverside esplanade he would propose at Buenos Aires three years later.
stops.campa: The fair is over and the ground it stood on is his to think about. He tells a newspaper what he means to do next: the esplanade of the Invalides, the Champ de Mars, and gardens and terraces along the embankments to lighten the severe stone ramparts that make the quays. The line of the river, he says, has a variety and a picturesqueness that will carry ornament, and the gardens he can see would run from the Trocadéro all the way to the Champ de Mars. Nobody has made enough of the Seine.
stops.quote: je compte amenager l'esplanade des Invalides, les Champs de Mars et les berges de la Seine. Je voudrais creer, sur ces berges, des jardins et des terrasses qui egayeraient un peu ce qu'ont de severe les remparts de pierre qui forment les quais. On n'a pas assez tire parti de la Seine, la ligne du fleuve est d'une variete et d'un pittoresque qui permettent des jolis motifs de deco. Les jardins que j'entrevois relieraient le Trocadero au Champs de Mars
stops.quote_source: Bouvard in Le Temps, 17 June 1904, p.458, reproduced in Alicia Novick, 'Planes versus proyectos', Revista de Urbanismo N.3, Universidad de Chile, 2000, p.9 n.31
sources: Alicia Novick, 'Planes versus proyectos', Revista de Urbanismo N.3, 2000, PDF fetched
suggested_refs: Le Temps, 17 June 1904, on Bouvard's projects for the Seine embankments

segments.name: Watercolours for Cities He Was Not Building

stops.name: The Hippodrome, a park drawn for the Sultan
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the two accounts conflict. Zeynep Çelik's 1984 article in JSAH, unreachable here since JSTOR and the University of California Press both returned 403, dates the Constantinople scheme to 1902 and holds that Bouvard never visited the city. fr.wikipedia dates the proposals to 1907 and says he discovered the city with his son Roger. The stop takes 1902 to order the segment and adjudicates nothing. The count of five watercolour proposals is the compilation tradition's and is a reconstruction like the rest.
stops.campa: Abdülhamid II wants his capital modernized, and a Frenchman is asked for drawings. Bouvard sends watercolours. On the old Hippodrome, where the chariots ran and the Ottoman court held its festivals, he lays out a landscaped park in geometric compartments with the obelisks standing in it like the ornaments of a French square. Five sheets go east to the palace and not one of them is built. Whether he ever stood on the ground he was redrawing is what the sources cannot agree on.
sources: Zeynep Çelik, 'Bouvard's Boulevards: Beaux-Arts Planning in Istanbul', JSAH 43 no. 4 (1984), unreachable (403), reported through the compilation tradition
fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph Bouvard', which dates the proposals to 1907 and has him seeing the city with his son
suggested_refs: Bouvard's Constantinople watercolours, Istanbul University Library

stops.name: Beyazıt Square, a civic centre in watercolour
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction resting on Çelik 1984, which could not be retrieved. The detail that the sultan and his court admired the drawings but found them too abstract and financially unrealistic rests entirely on that unread article and is softened here. The 1902 date is contested by fr.wikipedia's 1907, as at the previous stop.
stops.campa: Beyazıt he recasts as a monumental civic centre: a new municipal building, cultural institutions, the square regularized and its traffic composed around it in the Parisian manner. None of it is built. The court is said to have admired the sheets and found them too abstract for the ground and too expensive for the treasury, though that judgement reaches us only through a study nobody in this chain could open. The watercolours survive in the university library.
sources: Çelik 1984, via the compilation tradition; the article itself returned 403
suggested_refs: The Beyazıt Square sheets among Bouvard's Constantinople watercolours

stops.name: The Galata Bridge, the Pont Alexandre III moved east
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on Çelik 1984 and her book of 1986, neither retrieved; the formal borrowing from the Pont Alexandre III is her reading. The date is contested as at the two previous stops, and the pool's flat assertion that Bouvard never set foot in the city is contradicted by fr.wikipedia and is not repeated here as fact.
stops.campa: Across the Golden Horn he proposes a new bridge carrying the features of the one just thrown over the Seine for the fair of 1900, with boulevards running from it to the monumental nodes of the city. Constantinople is to be joined up the way Paris was joined up, by a man who had directed the architecture of a world's fair and had never governed a hill. The scheme dies on paper. Later French writing will call him the new Haussmann of the East for it.
sources: Çelik 1984 and Çelik, The Remaking of Istanbul (1986), neither fetched
suggested_refs: The Galata Bridge proposal in Bouvard's Constantinople portfolio

stops.name: Brussels, the approaches to the Palais de Justice
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the compilation tradition, apparently drawing on D'Elboux, records a request from Leopold II and a signed watercolour of 1904 said to compose the space against the Place de la Concorde. No Belgian municipal or royal archive was consulted. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: Leopold II, who is spending a fortune of Congo rubber on the rebuilding of his capital, asks Bouvard to study the approaches to Poelaert's enormous courthouse and the Porte de Namur. A watercolour comes back, reportedly composed against the Place de la Concorde. Nothing is executed. He is sixty-four, consulting abroad while still directing the services of Paris. The sheet is signed and dated 1904; what was asked of him and what he was paid are not in any archive consulted here.
sources: Compilation tradition drawing on D'Elboux; no Belgian archive consulted
suggested_refs: The signed 1904 watercolour of the Palais de Justice approaches, Brussels

segments.name: Buenos Aires: The Plan and Its Interruption

stops.name: Paris, the Argentine delegation and the offer
stops.date_confidence: attested as a quotation at one remove. D'Elboux's footnote 20 gives the source exactly: Le Temps, Paris, 9 December 1906, article Une autre entente municipale, rubric Au jour le jour. The original issue was not opened and only her Portuguese translation was accessible. That the mission was mediated by the journalist Henri Turot and sought by mayor Carlos Torcuato de Alvear is a reconstruction.
stops.campa: A municipal delegation from Buenos Aires comes to Paris and is entertained by the city it means to imitate. The Argentine capital is preparing for the centenary of its revolution and wants a European hand on its plan. The Paris press reports the arrangement as a piece of diplomacy: the mayor and the president have the right man to hand, the offer has been made, Bouvard has accepted, and he will sail within months. He is sixty-six and has never worked outside Europe.
stops.quote: O prefeito e o presidente tem, alem disso, junto a eles o homem certo para a grande tarefa a realizar. E M. Bouvard, a quem a oferta ja foi feita. Bouvard aceitou e ira, dentro de alguns meses, a Buenos Aires, estudar a organizacao da exposicao e a transformacao da cidade. Sua experiencia nessa materia e garantia certa do sucesso da empreitada.
stops.quote_source: Le Temps (Paris), 9 December 1906, 'Une autre entente municipale', in the Portuguese translation of Roseli Maria Martins D'Elboux, Revista Brasileira de História da Ciência 11(1), 2018, p.40 n.20
sources: D'Elboux 2018, PDF fetched and text-searched
Compilation tradition for Turot's mediation, unverified
suggested_refs: Le Temps, 9 December 1906, rubric Au jour le jour

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo, the capital turned toward its river
stops.date_confidence: the 1907 mission is attested, fr.wikipedia and es.wikipedia both giving a Buenos Aires urban plan of 1907-1909, and observatorioamba.org confirms that the plan addressed plazas, parks and monumental spaces. The month is uncertain and contested: the pool gives July 1907 for the crossing, but a Buenos Aires newspaper published his Plaza del Congreso scheme on 27 June 1907, which no source reconciles. The travelling architects Delattre and Faure-Dujarric appear in no reachable source.
stops.campa: He lands in a city of a million people laid out on a Spanish grid that turns its back on the water, and at the Plaza de Mayo he does what he had told a Paris newspaper he wanted to do on the Seine: open the ceremonial centre toward the river with an esplanade. The government house, the cathedral and the old cabildo stand around a square that stops dead at the customs works. Behind him is the whole apparatus of the City of Paris. Beyond the works lies the Plata, and there is no street that takes the square to it.
sources: observatorioamba.org, ficha for the 1910 Nuevo Plan para Buenos Aires
fr.wikipedia and es.wikipedia, for the 1907-1909 plan
suggested_refs: The Plaza de Mayo esplanade proposals among the associated projects of the Nuevo Plano

stops.name: Plaza del Congreso, the scheme published in the newspaper
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the article La futura Plaza del Congreso is dated 27 June 1907 in La Prensa by the compilation tradition and the original issue was not retrieved, though observatorioamba.org lists the Plaza del Congreso among the plan's associated projects. The date sits before the July arrival the pool gives, a conflict no source resolves. Coordinates inherited from the existing pin for this plaza.
stops.campa: The square before the national legislature is the piece of Buenos Aires everybody is drawing that year, and Bouvard publishes his version of it in a newspaper rather than filing it with the council: an axis, a composition, the congress building given a foreground worthy of it. La Prensa carries it on the twenty-seventh of June. Going to the readers rather than to the councillors puts the scheme where anyone with a rival one can answer it, and within a week somebody does.
sources: Compilation tradition citing La Prensa, 27 June 1907, issue not retrieved
observatorioamba.org, associated projects of the 1910 Nuevo Plan
suggested_refs: La Prensa, Buenos Aires, 27 June 1907, 'La futura Plaza del Congreso'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the diagonals attacked
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the attack by the architect Víctor Julio Jaeschke in El Tiempo on 2 July 1907 comes from Jorge Daniel Tartarini's study of the controversy and the issue was not retrieved. The 1908 interruption under Intendente Manuel J. Güiraldes is on the same footing. The quotation is at two removes: D'Elboux's footnote 32 names its source as Novick 2003, p.118, not a French diplomatic document, correcting the pool.
stops.campa: Days after the plaza scheme appears, a local architect answers it in another paper: the diagonals Bouvard wants driven across the grid will wreck what exists to buy an effect borrowed from Europe. The quarrel becomes public. Then the mayor who invited him leaves office, his successor suspends the contract, and a French voice warns that cancelling a commission the Republic had celebrated would be read in Paris as proof of an Argentine crisis. The contract is renegotiated instead of killed.
stops.quote: A missao pela qual o Sr. Bouvard foi convocado foi ocasiao, no ano passado, em Paris, de celebracoes as quais o Governo Republicano se envolveu plenamente. Nao seria perigoso que se atribuisse esse cancelamento a existencia de uma crise na Argentina, a qual M. Zeballos teve a precaucao de desmentir?
stops.quote_source: Quoted by Alicia Novick (2003), p.118, in the Portuguese rendering of Roseli Maria Martins D'Elboux, Revista Brasileira de História da Ciência 11(1), 2018, p.41 n.32
sources: D'Elboux 2018, PDF fetched
Jorge Daniel Tartarini's study of the Bouvard-Jaeschke controversy, via the compilation tradition
suggested_refs: El Tiempo, Buenos Aires, 2 July 1907, Jaeschke on the proposed diagonals

stops.name: La Isla, the streets and terraces of Recoleta
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance by arcondebuenosaires.com.ar, which credits the French architect José Bouvard, whom it calls Director of Parks of Paris, with the plan of the new quarter, the tracing of its streets and Plaza Mitre, and the terraces and staircases that characterize it. That source gives no year at all, so 1907 and the month are inference; and its title for him is a loose rendering of his actual post. Coordinates corrected to Plaza Mitre.
stops.campa: On the expropriated grounds of the Quinta Hale, above the barranca where the old shoreline ran, he lays out a quarter: streets traced along the high ground, a plaza set as a belvedere over the river, terraces and staircases carrying the ground down. The neighbours call it La Isla, the island, because the land stands up out of the city around it. Of everything he proposed in Argentina this is the piece that got built, and it got built as drawn. The staircases are still there.
sources: arcondebuenosaires.com.ar, Quinta Hale / Pearson page, fetched
suggested_refs: Plaza Mitre and the terraces of La Isla, Recoleta, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Nuevo Plano and its commission
stops.date_confidence: attested: observatorioamba.org's ficha confirms the commission of Carlos María Morales, Carlos Thays, Anastacio Iturbe, Fernando Pérez and Román Bravo, the span of 1907-1910 and the framing as a plan of embellishment and extension. Dropped as unsupported: the count of roughly thirty-two diagonals, which is in no source. That the plan leaned on Forestier, Hénard and Buls among its authorities is a reconstruction, unverified against the printed plan. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: The work is finished not by a foreign consultant alone but by a commission: Carlos María Morales, Anastacio Iturbe, Fernando Pérez, Román Bravo, and Carlos Thays, who has been planting the parks and plazas of this city for seventeen years and knows every tree in them. Out of it comes El nuevo plano de la ciudad de Buenos Aires, diagonals over the grid, a widened north-south avenue, works staged over years, leaning on Jean-Claude-Nicolas Forestier among the authorities it cites. It will be called the Plan Bouvard by everyone who never read its title page.
stops.quote: ante la diversidad de proyectos que se han hecho públicos (hace) de indiscutible utilidad hacer un estudio de conjunto
stops.quote_source: Intendencia Municipal, El Nuevo Plano, Buenos Aires, 1909, p.5, quoted in Alicia Novick, 'Planes versus proyectos', Revista de Urbanismo N.3, 2000, p.8 n.29; the bracketed (hace) is Novick's editorial insertion and is kept
sources: observatorioamba.org, ficha for the 1910 Nuevo Plan para Buenos Aires
Alicia Novick, 'Planes versus proyectos', 2000, PDF fetched
suggested_refs: carlos_thays.journey.json, for Thays's twenty-two years as Director de Paseos
jean_claude_nicolas_forestier.journey.json, for Forestier's own Buenos Aires commission of 1923-1925

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the plan printed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication: observatorioamba.org's ficha gives the printed title and the year 1910, with the imprint Imprenta Litografía y Encuadernación Kraft, correcting the pool's Talleres Gráficos de la Penitenciaría Nacional, and states no page count. The same source's bibliography garbles the author as Bouvard, Andrés, while its text calls him J. J. Bouvard. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: The report comes off a Buenos Aires press in the centenary year, bound with its plan: a document of embellishment and extension, arguing that what has been done so far, and above all in the densest part of the city, has pushed aside the beautiful aspects of the incomparable river along its edge. It will be quarried for fifty years by men who cite it far more often than they read it. The catalogues begin garbling him at once: Andrés Bouvard in one record, J. J. Bouvard in another.
stops.quote: Las disposiciones adoptadas hasta ahora, y, en particular en la parte mas densa de la ciudad, han hecho a un lado los hermosos aspectos del incomparable rio que la bordea
stops.quote_source: El Nuevo Plano de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, Buenos Aires, 1909, p.17, quoted in Alicia Novick, 'Planes versus proyectos', Revista de Urbanismo N.3, 2000, pp.8-9 n.31
sources: observatorioamba.org, ficha for the 1910 Nuevo Plan para Buenos Aires
Alicia Novick, 'Planes versus proyectos', 2000
suggested_refs: El nuevo plano de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, Imprenta Kraft, 1910

segments.name: The Consulting Years: Antwerp, Rosario, Montevideo

stops.name: Antwerp, the competition he cannot judge
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, per D'Elboux's account, which was not fetched in full; no Belgian competition record was consulted. The pool records a comparable consultation at Bayonne in 1909 on the same footing, not carried here as its own stop. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: Antwerp opens an international competition for its extension and puts the Frenchman in the chair. Then a ministry rules that the jury must be Belgian, and he is replaced. The competition is won by Henri Prost, who had been his student. He is invited from abroad because the prestige of Paris travels, and he is removed the moment a Belgian ministry decides that a Belgian plan should be settled by Belgians. He is seventy, and the winning entry is his pupil's.
sources: Compilation tradition citing D'Elboux's reconstruction, not fetched
suggested_refs: The Antwerp extension competition of 1910 and Henri Prost's winning entry

stops.name: Rosario, a few days and a report
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Rosario episode rests on the planning-history studies of García Ortúzar, Berjman and Tartarini, none of them retrieved here. The pool gives a stay of a few days between June and October 1910, after repeated proposals by council member José Martinoli and an invitation from mayor Isidro Quiroga; October places the stop.
stops.campa: The second Argentine city, growing on grain and its port, wants what the capital had. A councillor has been proposing it for years, the mayor invites him, and Bouvard comes up the Paraná, spends a few days and writes a report on diagonals, a civic composition, the relation of port to centre, and circulation. Rosario files it and builds a fraction of it, the way cities do with embellishment plans. How long he actually stayed reaches us as a few days, with no dates attached to them.
sources: Compilation tradition citing García Ortúzar and Berjman on Rosario, and Tartarini; cdsa.aacademica.org not retrieved
suggested_refs: The 1910 Rosario embellishment report and the municipal debates around it

stops.name: Montevideo, a plan that may not exist
stops.date_confidence: unresolved attribution, carried as such. French and Brazilian compilations credit Bouvard with an embellishment plan for Montevideo, and nothing reachable establishes whether he produced a commissioned plan, gave advice, or has been conflated with the city's separate international avenues competition. The year is the pool's and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Across the estuary, the compilations say, he also drew Montevideo. Whether he was engaged, whether he merely advised, whether somebody later confused his name with the international competition the city ran for its avenues: the record does not say. Somebody in Paris writes the entry, somebody in Brazil copies it, and a city enters the list of his works without a client and without a drawing that anybody has produced. No source reached in this research settles it.
sources: French and Brazilian biographical compilations, unspecified in the pool and unconfirmed by any source fetched
suggested_refs: Montevideo municipal records of the early 1910s on the avenues competition

stops.name: Paris, the order that retires him
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the prefectural order making him honorary director is carried by the compilation tradition and its text was not seen.
stops.campa: A prefectural order takes him off the active strength of the City of Paris, forty-seven years after a young draftsman from Vienne was attached to its architecture service, and makes him honorary director. Within days he is on a ship for Brazil with a Belgian banker, going into business on the other side of the Atlantic in the field he had spent a whole career administering for a municipality. He has been on the municipal payroll since the Second Empire. He is seventy-one.
sources: Compilation tradition; no prefectural order text located
suggested_refs: Prefectural orders of the Seine, March 1911, Archives de Paris

stops.name: Curitiba, the banker's expedition
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Curitiba episode comes from D'Elboux's thesis, whose body text could not be read, and the fetched abstract does not mention it. The pool places the Brazilian departure around the retirement order of 10 March 1911; the day used here is a placeholder that orders the crossing after it.
stops.campa: Édouard Fontaine de Laveleye holds the tramways, the paving and the electric distribution of Curitiba, and brings Bouvard to sell the city an improvement plan drawn by the man who ran the fair of 1900. The reception is cool. A Paraná capital of a hundred thousand does not need a Champ-de-Mars, and a concessionaire who owns the utilities proposing to redraw the streets is a proposition the councillors can read for themselves. They go on to São Paulo.
sources: D'Elboux's thesis on Bouvard in South America, abstract fetched at teses.usp.br, body not read
suggested_refs: Curitiba municipal records of 1911 on the Laveleye concessions

stops.name: Vale do Anhangabaú, the valley kept as a park
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The invitation from the public-works director Victor da Silva Freire, the two months in the city and the municipal resolution of 16 June 1911 all come from the compilation tradition; pt.wikipedia's Vale do Anhangabaú confirms only that important remodelling proposals emerged between 1910 and 1911, naming neither man, and the pool's citation of pt.wikipedia's Companhia City for this report was a mis-sourcing, since that page says nothing of it.
stops.campa: São Paulo is arguing with itself about the valley that splits it, and the director of public works calls in a referee. Bouvard spends about two months and finds the compromise: the Anhangabaú stays a park, a connected green that receives the roads instead of being turned into one. The city approves the report. In the decades after, the valley will be paved, tunnelled, roofed over and dug up again, and every generation of paulistano planners will argue about it with his answer somewhere in the file.
sources: pt.wikipedia, 'Vale do Anhangabaú', which confirms only the 1910-1911 proposals without naming Bouvard or Freire
Compilation tradition citing D'Elboux
suggested_refs: The 1911 São Paulo municipal resolution on the Anhangabaú valley

stops.name: The City of London, the company constituted
stops.date_confidence: split evidence. Attested by pt.wikipedia's Companhia City: founded in 1911 with initial headquarters in London and French, English and Brazilian investors, established definitively in São Paulo in 1912, acquiring more than 15 million square metres, with Barry Parker and Raymond Unwin responsible for the layout of Jardim América on an original plan of 1919. Not in that source, and therefore reconstruction: Boulton Brothers, Lord Balfour of Burleigh, Laveleye, Bouvard's organizing role and his vice-chairmanship until his death. The company history behind the date gives two competing days, 11 and 25 September 1911.
stops.campa: In an office in the City, British money constitutes the City of São Paulo Improvements and Freehold Land Company. The old municipal architect, who had spent forty-seven years laying out public funds on public ground, is now on the other side of the table: land assembled, a company floated, more than fifteen million square metres bought in a city he had seen once. The garden suburbs are drawn later by Barry Parker and Raymond Unwin, on an original plan of 1919. He is vice-chairman of the company until he dies. Its own history gives two different days for the founding, the eleventh and the twenty-fifth of September 1911.
sources: pt.wikipedia, 'Companhia City', for the 1911 London foundation, the 1912 São Paulo establishment, the 15 million square metres and the Parker and Unwin plan of 1919
Unnamed company history for the constitution dates, not fetched
suggested_refs: The registration file of the City of São Paulo Improvements and Freehold Land Co. Ltd, London, September 1911

stops.name: Pacaembu, the subdivision abandoned
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: D'Elboux's thesis on the company's early years, whose body was not read. The span of 1911 to 1916 for the scheme and its abandonment is hers; the stop is placed at the abandonment and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: For the company he conceives the first Pacaembu, a subdivision on the hills northwest of the centre. Survey lines go in, earth is moved, and in 1916 the scheme is dropped. The company turns to easier land, and the hills wait twenty years for another plan. The neighbourhood that eventually rises there is somebody else's drawing laid over the first cuts of his. What is left of the original is Rua Traipu, wider than it needs to be, holding the alignment of an avenue that was never built.
sources: Compilation tradition citing D'Elboux's thesis on the early years of the Cia. City
suggested_refs: Rua Traipu, São Paulo, and the abandoned first Pacaembu survey

stops.name: Marly-le-Roi, death in the house
stops.date_confidence: attested that he died at Marly-le-Roi, then Seine-et-Oise, at the age of eighty; the day is contested and unresolved. fr.wikipedia gives 5 November 1920 and the INHA civil-act tradition gives 4 November 1920, both descending from documentary sources, and nothing consulted adjudicates. The 4 November reading is used here without preference. No burial place was found in any source consulted, which is recorded as a gap and not filled by inference.
stops.campa: He dies at home, in the house at Marly-le-Roi where his son was born forty-five years earlier, aged eighty. One documentary tradition gives the fourth of November and another gives the fifth, and neither yields. Where he is buried is not recorded anywhere this research could reach: not in the encyclopaedias, and not in the theses that rebuilt his South American decade out of company minutes and diplomatic correspondence. The grave is simply not known.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Joseph Bouvard', giving 5 November 1920
INHA civil-act tradition giving 4 November 1920, via the compilation tradition; agorha.inha.fr returned 403
suggested_refs: The civil death register of Marly-le-Roi, November 1920

stops.name: Paris, the obituary in La Construction moderne
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the obituary in La Construction moderne of 28 November 1920 is reported by the compilation tradition and the issue was not retrieved. The stop sits at the canonical Paris pin, the place of publication.
stops.campa: Three weeks after the death the architectural press notices it. A man who had been the administrative head of everything built by the largest municipality in France is marked in the professional papers and nowhere else that can be traced. La Construction moderne prints the notice on the twenty-eighth of November, a column among the drawings of other men's buildings. Of his private life, then or since, nothing has been written that this research could find.
sources: Compilation tradition citing La Construction moderne, 28 November 1920; issue not retrieved
suggested_refs: La Construction moderne, 28 November 1920, obituary of Joseph-Antoine Bouvard

stops.name: Avenue Joseph-Bouvard, the name on the Champ-de-Mars
stops.date_confidence: attested: fr.wikipedia's Avenue Joseph-Bouvard gives the naming decision of 18 March 1921, the dimensions of 450 metres by 50, the run from the Place du Général-Gouraud to 35 avenue de Suffren, and the quoted description of the honorand. Coordinates corrected to that article's own figures. The detachment of a roundabout as Place Jacques-Rueff in 1984 is attested by the same article.
stops.campa: Four months after his death the city gives him four hundred and fifty metres of the Champ-de-Mars, the field where he had built the pavilion of 1878 and the dome of 1889, and where the tower he was set against still stands. The record names him administrative director of the services of architecture, promenades and plantations of the City of Paris. In 1984 a roundabout is detached from it and named for Jacques Rueff. What is left runs from the Place du Général-Gouraud to number 35 avenue de Suffren.
stops.quote: directeur administratif des services d'architecture, des promenades et plantations de la ville de Paris
stops.quote_source: The City of Paris description of the honorand, naming decision of 18 March 1921, per fr.wikipedia, 'Avenue Joseph-Bouvard'
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Avenue Joseph-Bouvard'
suggested_refs: Avenue Joseph-Bouvard and Place Jacques-Rueff, Champ-de-Mars, Paris 7e
